title: Crypto Debit vs. Prepaid vs. Credit Cards: Fees, Custody & Tax Differences Explained
seoTitle: Crypto Debit vs. Prepaid vs. Credit Cards (2026): Fees & Taxes
excerpt: How do crypto cards work? Compare crypto debit, prepaid, revolving credit and DeFi collateral cards on conversion spreads, self-custody and capital-gains tax triggers.

mainImage.alt: Three glass payment cards representing crypto debit, prepaid and collateralized credit cards - coins streaming out of one, loading into another, and locked in a vault beside the third

keyTakeaways: Every crypto card settles fiat to the merchant over Visa or Mastercard rails. The real differences are when your crypto converts, who holds custody, and which tax events trigger.

Debit converts at the point of sale (a capital gain per swipe), prepaid converts at top-up (up to 3% load fees and a taxable disposal before you shop), revolving credit never sells your crypto, and collateralized lines borrow against it.
Self-custody smart accounts keep your USDC or ETH in your own wallet until checkout authorization; custodial cards leave you as an unsecured creditor if the issuer freezes withdrawals.
A '$0 monthly fee' card can still cost $18 to $60 on a $2,000 monthly spend once conversion spreads and FX markups are counted.
Collateralized credit-line cards like ether.fi Cash, Nexo and Avici defer capital gains because borrowing against crypto is not a disposal - until your collateral is liquidated.

children.text: Every crypto payment card bridges digital assets to the traditional Visa, Mastercard or American Express merchant rails, because merchants always receive local fiat currency at the point of sale - never cryptocurrency. Whether you tap a physical card or Apple Pay, the terminal requests dollars or euros and a chain of issuers, processors and smart contracts decides how to fund it. What actually separates the four card architectures is when your crypto is sold, who holds custody of your balance, how much the conversion or cashback really costs, and which taxable events each swipe triggers. The four models:
) convert crypto or stablecoins to fiat in real time at the exact second of checkout - a capital gain or loss per swipe, unless you spend 1:1 USD-pegged stablecoins.
) require pre-loading a segregated card balance. Converting BTC or ETH into fiat or stablecoins at load time charges a top-up fee of up to 3% and crystallizes a taxable disposal before you ever shop.
) work like ordinary bank credit cards: you borrow fiat, repay in cash each month and earn 1-4% in crypto rewards. Nothing is sold, so no capital gains trigger at checkout.
) lock BTC, ETH or USDC as collateral and let you borrow spending liquidity - so you spend without selling principal or triggering a taxable disposal.

children.text: How crypto payment cards actually work: the 4-step settlement flow

When you tap a crypto card at a terminal or in Apple Pay, four things happen in under three seconds. Understanding this flow explains why 'spending crypto' is really 'selling crypto at the checkout' for debit and prepaid cards - and why credit-line cards escape that tax event entirely.
You tap at any of the 150M+ Visa or Mastercard merchants. The terminal requests payment in local fiat - EUR, USD, GBP - and knows nothing about crypto.
The payment processor and licensed BIN sponsor - issuers like
- receive the fiat request and identify which programme and funding account it belongs to.

A debit card swaps your crypto at the point of sale, a prepaid card deducts from a balance you already loaded, and a credit-line card posts the charge against your collateralized limit. This is the step where fees and tax events are born.

The merchant receives 100% standard fiat over the card network rails and never touches cryptocurrency. Your statement may say 'coffee,' but the ledger behind it is either a crypto sale, a balance debit or a loan.

children.text: Crypto debit vs. prepaid cards: real-time conversion vs. top-up spreads

Marketing blurs the line between 'debit' and 'prepaid' - issuers call almost everything a debit card. The mechanical difference matters to your wallet: a true debit card leaves funds in your main balance until the second you pay, while a prepaid card forces you to move value into a separate, provider-held card balance first.
A true debit card is connected directly to a funding account - either an exchange balance (
) or a wallet under your own keys (
). Funds sit in your main balance - earning yield or simply remaining yours - until you swipe. The conversion happens at the point of sale at the spot rate, minus whatever spread the issuer charges.

Pro tip: Bybit Card spends fiat first. If you hold EUR or GBP in your Bybit Funding Account, the card draws the fiat balance and sidesteps the crypto conversion fee entirely. The trade-off: fiat-funded purchases on Bybit Global do not earn cashback points.
Crypto prepaid mechanics - and the prepaid trap
A prepaid card makes you move funds into a segregated card wallet first -

all work this way. Two consequences follow. First, the conversion happens at load time, which is when top-up fees apply (BitPay charges 3% to preload USD from your wallet) and when a volatile-crypto disposal crystallizes for tax purposes - before you buy anything. Second, the prepaid trap: once value is loaded onto many prepaid programmes it cannot be transferred back out to an on-chain wallet. Your exit is spending it.

Tax implications (IRS Form 1099-DA & 8949): when does a card swipe trigger capital gains?

Under IRS Notice 2014-21, crypto is property - so spending it is a disposal, just like selling it. Revenue Procedure 2024-28 adds mandatory per-wallet cost-basis tracking, and brokers now report disposals on Form 1099-DA. Here is what each architecture does to your tax return:
Spending volatile crypto on a debit card (BTC, ETH, SOL):
every coffee or subscription renewal is a taxable property disposal. You owe Form 8949 and Schedule D math on each swipe: capital gain = proceeds at checkout minus original cost basis.
converting BTC to USD - or even swapping BTC for USDT - to top up triggers the capital gain at the moment of the load, before you buy anything.
technically still a property disposal in the US, but spending USDC acquired at $1.00 produces a ~$0.00 gain or loss - you still reconcile the 1099-DA, yet there is no surprise tax bill.

loan proceeds are not taxable income and no asset is sold at checkout, so borrowing against your crypto defers capital gains indefinitely - unless your collateral is liquidated, which is itself a forced disposal.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a crypto debit card and a crypto prepaid card?
faqs.answer: A crypto debit card pulls from your main wallet or exchange balance and converts to fiat in real time at the point of sale. A prepaid card requires loading a segregated card balance first - which charges top-up fees of up to 3% and triggers a taxable disposal at load time if you convert volatile crypto.

faqs.question: Do crypto credit cards require a credit check?
faqs.answer: US revolving credit cards like the Gemini Credit Card and Coinbase One Card require a real credit check because a bank is lending you fiat. Collateralized credit-line cards like Nexo, ether.fi Cash and Avici require only crypto collateral and standard KYC - no hard credit pull.

faqs.question: Which type of crypto card avoids capital gains taxes when spending?
faqs.answer: Collateralized credit-line cards let you borrow against BTC or ETH without selling, so no disposal occurs at checkout. Spending 1:1 USD-pegged stablecoins like USDC on a debit card is a close second - technically a disposal, but with roughly $0 gain or loss per swipe.

faqs.question: Can I switch between debit mode and credit mode on the same crypto card?
faqs.answer: Yes - dual-mode cards like the Nexo Card let you toggle in-app between spending your balance directly (debit mode) and borrowing against collateral (credit mode). Solid, Exa and XPlace offer similar mode-switching between direct spending and collateralized credit.
